approach: Retrospective cohort study. Patients receiving ICIs for advanced/metastatic disease between Jan 2018 and Dec 2023 were grouped based on infusion timing relative to the median time of all treatments ('early group': <50% cycles after median time; 'late group': ≥50%). Primary endpoint was OS. Multivariable-adjusted Hazard Ratios (HRs) were estimated using standard Cox models and time-dependent Cox models to account for potential changes in group assignment over time. Sensitivity analyses were performed.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides evidence from a large sample size suggesting a benefit in OS with early ICI administration, utilizing time-dependent Cox models to reduce immortal time bias.
contribution_and_limits.limits: Retrospective design limits causal inference; results may be specific to the single-centre setting; no difference found when chemotherapy is included; sensitivity analysis results varied by model type.

key_findings.finding: Median OS was significantly shorter in the late group (13.1 months) compared to the early group (21.4 months). Time-dependent Cox model showed HR 1.30 (95% CI 1.16-1.44) for death in the late group.

key_findings.conditions: Regimens with ICIs alone (n=1886) or ICIs plus tyrosine kinase inhibitors (n=163)
key_findings.finding: The association between later administration and shorter OS remained significant.
No significant difference in OS was observed between early and late groups.

key_findings.conditions: Sensitivity analysis based on exposure at 3 months
key_findings.finding: Standard model showed no difference (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.98-1.20); time-dependent model showed higher risk of death for late group (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.02-1.26).

problem_or_question: To determine if the time of day of ICI infusion affects treatment response and overall survival in patients with advanced solid tumours, addressing limitations of previous small-scale studies with methodological biases.
research_scope: Advanced solid tumours (lung cancer, melanoma, renal carcinoma, head and neck, urothelial cancer) treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) at a large tertiary cancer centre; retrospective cohort analysis.
work_summary: This study investigates whether the timing of ICI administration influences overall survival (OS), based on evidence of circadian dependence in the immune system. Using a large single-centre cohort of 2631 patients, the authors compared outcomes between 'early' and 'late' treatment groups, defined by whether ≥50% of cycles were administered after the median infusion time. The analysis employed Cox models with and without time-dependent variables to mitigate immortal time bias, adjusting for age, sex, ECOG status, cancer type, and treatment regimen.
